amendments.rule: Reordered or discontinuous target tokens may occupy one unit when they realize one source item. Do not absorb unrelated intervening words into that unit. **Where English repeats one source function word because its scope is distributed across coordinated or emphatically repeated phrases or clauses, every English occurrence belongs to that source morpheme's one possibly discontinuous unit.** `מִן` in `מִבּוֹא בְדָמִים וְהוֹשֵׁעַ` → *from bloodguiltiness, and from avenging* takes both occurrences of *from*, while the waw takes only *and*; `בִּי אֲנִי` → *upon me ... upon me* gives both occurrences of *upon* to the single preposition while the suffix and explicit pronoun take their respective *me*. The repeated English word is neither `added` nor reassigned to a neighboring source item merely to make the units contiguous. **An explicit personal pronoun is read the same way where the ASV resumes it in a later clause of the same verse.** Where a following verbless clause writes no subject of its own and the ASV supplies the subject pronoun that an explicit `הוּא`, `הֵמָּה`, `אֲנִי` or the like standing earlier in the verse denotes, both occurrences belong to that pronoun's one discontinuous unit, exactly as rule 18 gives both pronouns of a twice-rendered suffix to the suffix and rule 20 gives both halves of an identifying formula to its one `הוּא`: `הֵמָּה סֹחֲרֵי יָדֵךְ ... בָּם סֹחֲרָיִךְ` → *they were the merchants of thy hand ... in these were* ***they*** *thy merchants* gives both *they*s to the one `הֵמָּה`, headed on the first. Such a pronoun is not `added`, and it does not join the predicate's unit: rule 20 hands the predicate the construction's copula and, in a presentative clause, its dummy *there*, and a referential pronoun is neither, so the clause's supplied *were* goes to the predicate while the pronoun goes to the morpheme that denotes it. This governs a clause with no subject of its own: where a finite verb stands in the resumed clause it takes the English subject pronoun under rule 17, which is a pronoun realizing that verb's own person and number. **And where the Hebrew stands the pronoun is not part of the condition.** Hebrew postposes an explicit subject pronoun after its predicate and that predicate's adjuncts, often before a coordinated second subject, while English writes a subject before its verb; where the ASV writes the pronoun in both places it has realized one written morpheme twice, and both occurrences are that pronoun's one discontinuous unit, headed on the first English occurrence: `וְהִנֵּה נִצָּב עַל־עֹלָתוֹ הוּא וְכָל־שָׂרֵי מוֹאָב` → *and lo* ***he*** *was standing by his burnt offering,* ***he*** *and all the princes of Moab* gives both *he*s to the one `הוּא`, while `נִצָּב` keeps the *was standing* rule 20 leaves it and the coordinated subject keeps its own English. So read whether one written pronoun is realized twice rather than which side of the resumption it stands on, and do not hand the first occurrence to the predicate to make the units contiguous: rule 17's permission reaches a pronoun realizing a finite verb's own person and number, and a participle or other predicate morpheme in a verbless clause takes only the copula. **And the morpheme that denotes the resumed subject need not be a pronoun.** Where a common noun or a proper name written in the verse is the referent the ASV resumes, every English realization of that referent belongs to the noun's one possibly discontinuous unit on exactly the terms above, headed on the first English occurrence: `עַל־אֱלוֹהַּ נוֹרָא הוֹד` → ***God*** *hath upon* ***him*** *terrible majesty* gives both *God* and *him* to the one `אֱלוֹהַּ`, and `שַׁדַּי לֹא־מְצָאנֻהוּ שַׂגִּיא־כֹּחַ` → *Touching* ***the Almighty****, we cannot find him out;* ***He*** *is excellent in power* gives the resuming *He* to `שַׁדַּי`, while `שַׂגִּיא` keeps the *is excellent* rule 20 leaves it. This is the preceding paragraphs' own reasoning read for the morpheme that is actually written — the pronoun goes to the morpheme that denotes it — since what licenses the English word is that the verse writes the referent, and not the part of speech the ASV first realized it by. Rule 17's ruling that a supplied lexical subject noun is `added` does not reach such a pronoun: that ruling governs an English noun answering to no morpheme at all, as `יָשְׁבוּ בָהּ` → *men shall dwell therein* is, and here a written nominal answers to it, so read whether the verse writes the referent before marking a supplied subject `added` or folding it into the predicate under rule 20. **But a morpheme already holding a pronoun of its own is not a home for a second one.** Where more than one morpheme in the verse denotes that referent, each takes only the English written for it, as rule 51 says of a waw and rule 43 of a spent preposition: the object suffix of `מְצָאנֻהוּ` above takes the *him* of *find him out* under rule 18, and the further *He* goes to `שַׁדַּי`. Count the ASV's realizations against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s. **An interrogative particle or a negative whose scope covers coordinated clauses is read the same way.** Where the Hebrew writes `הֲ` or `לֹא` once in the first of two coordinated clauses and the ASV rewrites it at the head of the second, every occurrence belongs to that one morpheme's discontinuous unit, headed on the first: `הֲלוֹא מַחֲזֵה־שָׁוְא חֲזִיתֶם וּמִקְסַם כָּזָב אֲמַרְתֶּם` → ***Have*** *ye* ***not*** *seen a false vision, and* ***have*** *ye* ***not*** *spoken a lying divination* gives both *have*s to the `הֲ` and both *not*s to the `לֹא`, while each verb keeps only its own subject pronoun and lexical verb. This is rule 55's reading of a subordinator the ASV rewrites over a coordinated clause, applied to the particle that governs one. The second occurrence is neither `added` under rule 30 nor folded into the second clause's verb under rule 17. **Where in that first clause the morpheme stands is no part of the condition, and neither is a repetition of the same English word.** What licenses the second occurrence is that the morpheme's scope reaches the second clause, so a negative predicating of a verbless clause governs a coordinated colon from the middle of the first as readily as from its head, and the ASV answers it with whatever word carries the negation where that colon opens — a *Nor* or a *neither* as readily as a second *not*. `שְׂאֵת פְּנֵי־רָשָׁע לֹא־טוֹב לְהַטּוֹת צַדִּיק בַּמִּשְׁפָּט` → *To respect the person of the wicked is* ***not*** *good,* ***Nor*** *to turn aside the righteous in judgment* gives both *not* and *Nor* to the one `לֹא`, headed on the first. Read the clause's scope rather than the morpheme's position, exactly as rule 51 reads a postposed *also*, and do not mark such a word `added` under rule 14's closing sentences because no conjunction stands in the second colon: what that count marks is a coordinator no morpheme answers to, and what distinguishes a *Nor* from a bare *and* is the negation the written negative is there to license, as rule 35 says in heading such a word on the negative. An ASV italic on such a word corroborates it and decides nothing, by rule 7. But read what is actually written before applying it: where the Hebrew gaps the morpheme in the second line and a waw stands there, and the ASV writes a single word carrying both the coordination and the negation, rule 35 governs and that word goes to the waw, as `לֹא עֲלִיתֶם ... וַתִּגְדְּרוּ` → *Ye have not gone up ..., neither built up* leaves the *neither* to the waw alone; and where no conjunction morpheme stands in that colon at all, rule 35's fusion has no coordination to rest on and the distributed reading above governs.
amendments.why: PRO.18.5 met the case rule 25's negative sentence had not considered. `לֹא` stands mid-clause as the predicate negation of `שְׂאֵת פְּנֵי־רָשָׁע לֹא־טוֹב`, not at the head of the first clause, and the ASV answers its scope over the second colon with an italic *Nor* rather than a second *not* — so the sentence as written fitted neither on its position condition nor on its 'repeated English word' phrasing, and a later pass could have marked the word `added` under rule 14's closing sentences or reached for rule 35's fusion, which wants a waw the colon does not have. The amendment widens the condition to scope rather than position, says the second English word need not repeat the first, and closes the gap by naming the no-waw case explicitly against rule 35's own limit. Nothing else in the rule is altered, and the shape recurs throughout Hebrew poetry, where a negated first colon is answered by a bare *Nor* or *neither*.

conventions: Supplied italic verb in a colon whose Hebrew writes none: test three things in this order before placing it. First, whether the Hebrew writes that verb elsewhere in the coordination — PRO.18.3's second 'cometh' is the written בָּא realized twice and belongs to that verb's discontinuous unit under rule 34, not added. Second, whether a predicate morpheme stands in the colon for the word to link — PRO.18.12's 'goeth' links עֲנָוָה to the written prepositional predicate לִפְנֵי כָבוֹד and adds no participant, so it is rule 20's expanded copula and joins that preposition's unit under rule 49. Third, only where the word introduces an event, and often an argument, the Hebrew never wrote is it added: PRO.18.17 'pleadeth', PRO.18.19 'to be won', PRO.18.24 'doeth it'. The italic corroborates and decides none of them (rule 7).

Construct chains rendered as English possessives (PRO.18.4, 18.6, 18.7, 18.11, 18.16): the phrase's single determiner stands before the possessor's own word and belongs to the possessor's unit under rule 29, the construct keeping only its own word — 'A fool's lips', 'A fool's mouth', 'A man's gift', 'a man's mouth'. PRO.18.11 is the case to get right: the possessor is an anarthrous substantival adjective, so עָשִׁיר takes the whole 'The rich man's' — the determiner under rule 29, the supplied generic 'man' under rule 31 with the head staying on 'rich', and the possessive — while הוֹן takes the bare 'wealth'. A construct takes a determiner of its own only where the ASV writes a second one, as PRO.18.4's 'The words of a man's mouth' does.

report: Read all 24 verses end to end and all 34 candidate lemma groups. Every multi-treatment bucket is licensed by what the ASV writes or by the source morphology, so no patch is returned.

Function-morpheme candidates resolved: בְּ is 'are in' at 18.21 because it heads a prepositional predicate (rule 49) and unrepresented at 18.17 because the ASV promotes its object to the object of the supplied 'pleadeth' (rule 40); לְ is unrepresented at 18.7, where the dative is recast as the possessive 'his', and written 'unto'/'for' at 18.13 and 18.16; הַ is a written 'The' at 18.18, an assimilated article with no 'the' written at 18.5, and the substantival 'He that' at 18.17 (rule 41); שָׂפָה is a host noun at 18.7 and a nomen rectum at 18.20; בֶּטֶן is rendered at 18.20 and unrendered inside חַדְרֵי־בָטֶן at 18.8.

The chapter's one real theme is the ASV's supplied italic verb in a parallel colon, and it is handled by a consistent order of tests: 18.3's second 'cometh' is the written בָּא realized twice across the coordination (rule 34); 18.12's 'goeth' links a written prepositional predicate and adds no participant, so it is rule 20's expanded copula placed on לִפְנֵי by rule 49; 18.17 'pleadeth', 18.19 'to be won' and 18.24 'doeth it' each introduce an event the Hebrew never wrote and are added. Recorded as a convention.

Supplied determiners are uniform: 'such' (18.19), 'many' (18.24) and every supplied 'the' join the nominal they determine and never head it; the two supplied 'his own' runs (18.1, 18.24) are added for want of any suffix, while 18.11's 'his own' goes to the suffix that is written. 18.1's 'And' is added because no waw stands in that verse at all, and 18.5's italic 'Nor' is the written לֹא distributed over the second colon — a consistent pair, and the second case is what the rule 25 amendment below records.

Possessive chains (18.4, 18.6, 18.7, 18.11, 18.16) all put the phrase's single determiner on the possessor's word under rule 29, and 18.4 alone writes a second determiner, which goes to the outer construct. 18.20's swap — 'A man's' realizing the suffix on בִּטְנוֹ and 'his' realizing אִישׁ, the rectum of פִי — keeps each possessor morpheme with the noun it possesses and agrees with 18.4's reading of the same פִי־אִישׁ.

Head choices for two-word substantive renderings are uniform on rule 31's subtraction: 'dainty morsels' (18.8), 'sound wisdom' (18.1), 'innermost parts' (18.8), 'great men' (18.16), 'good thing' (18.22), 'The rich man's' (18.11) all head on the lexeme-bearing word, and each names the class-noun reading in its note under rule 8.

All six BSB disagreements are documented convention differences, not errors. 18.1 לְ, 18.7 לְ and 18.17 בְּ are prepositions the ASV's recasting leaves with no English word (rule 40); 18.9 הוּא is the resumptive pronoun of a tripartite clause the ASV realizes once (rules 20, 22); 18.14 נָּה is an object suffix the ASV writes no pronoun for ('who can bear'); 18.8 בָטֶן is unrendered because the ASV writes 'the innermost parts' and stops, and since חֶדֶר keeps 'innermost' of its own, rule 30's one-rendering fusion is unmet and rule 22 governs. None should be changed.

Two data notes for a later reader, neither an alignment defect: the ASV target for 18.8 ends at 'the innermost parts', with no 'of the belly' to align; and MACULA's glosses for 18.11 s011/s012 are the reversed pair rule 39 describes ('his own' printed on מַשְׂכִּית, 'imagination' on the suffix). The verse reads the morphology and aligns them correctly.
